Hidden Markov model is proposed based-on a simple notion: we are only able to observe a small protion of the whole world and the underlying mechanisms that generate such observables are hidden. For example, we can observe the weather of each day without being aware of the complicated xxx.

However, being not able to fully understand the latent mechanisms, we still want to be able to summarize general principles from previous observations and be able to predict future observations. For this purpose, the Hidden Markov model (HMM) was proposed.

Hidden Markov model is divided into two parts:
The hidden part where the state of the system evolves dynamically following certain rules;
and the observable part where we can observe the emitted signals depending on the state of the hidden system.

The transition of the states of the hidden system is described as a Markov chain, where the state in the current time step follows a distribution that is solely determined by the state in the previous time step. This property that the current state depends only on state one step before, but not more previous steps is called the Markov property.

In short, hidden Markov model endows a Markov chain modeling the hidden system, and a rule on how the state of the hidden system determines the observable.


Let's use a simple example to make these abstract descriptions to life.

Suppose that there is a family bakery in your neighborhood. Each day you pass by the bakery and on some days, the bakery sells delicious special cookies. Since you absolutely don't want to miss these treats, you take notes everyday about whether the cookies are being sold on that day.

Therefore, you have from day 1 to day $\tau$ a series of numbers:
$$0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, ..., 0$$,
where $0$ means the corresponding day there was no cookie and $1$ means the there were cookies sold.

Let's denote the value in this series on day $t$ as $X_t$. Hence, $X_t$ is our **observation** on day $t$.

But what determines whether cookies is sold? This is hidden behind the counter for a cookie-loving customer. Apparently, the family in the bakery take turns to be the chief baker on each day.

The family members include Jenny, her grandma, her mom and her dad. Whoever was the chief baker the day before decides who takes the chief position the current day.

The rule of transition is determined by the following graph:

::: {.cell}
![Graph for transition of baking position](./images/family_graph.png){width=60% fig-align="center" fig-cap="A scenic mountain view"}
:::

The nodes in the graph represent each family member. The weights on the edges represent the possibility of transition from one person to another.
For example, if Grandma was the chief baker on day $t-1$, then on day $t$, there will be 0.6 chance that Mum is the chief baker and 0.4 chance Jenney will be the chief baker.

With this rule, it is possible to have a sequence of the chief bakers from day 1 to day $\tau$ as follows:
$$Mum, Grandma, Jenny, Dad, Dad, Grandma, ..., Jenny$$.
Let's denote the chief baker on day $t$ as $S_t$. We can call $S_t$ the **hidden state** of the bakery on day $t$.

Now we modeled how the hidden state transitions as a Markov chain. The last thing we need is to model how the hidden state $S_t$, i.e. the chief baker, decides on the observable $X_t$, i.e. whether there will be cookies baked.
